doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Marshall Royal as a lead player and the Basie rehearsal story
summary: He praises Royal's leadership and tells of sitting in with Basie's band where Royal called out Ernie Wilkins.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: What was Marshall Royal like? Was he an exacting straw boss?

Well he was a straw boss, you got that right. I don’t know, I love Marshall. Marshall never really dictated, Marshall did it the way a real lead player should do it, and it’s the way I’ve always advocated. You shouldn’t have to tell people anything. You just play it the way you want it and they should follow you. And that’s what he did. And everybody had enough respect for him that they did it. To be very honest with you I didn’t agree © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

with everything Marshall played. I mean the way he played is not my style of playing. And I didn’t listen to him that much when I was a kid, I was listening to other people and a little, you know like maybe Bud Shank at that time or Vinnie Dean or Lee Konitz, that kind of thing he did with Stan or even the tenor players with Woody’s band. But I knew what Marshall was and what he had done and I certainly would have done anything he wanted me to do, to play with him in that regard. And we were good friends and we got along very well and it was a nice relationship. But I’ve got to tell you a funny story. When I was still on Maynard’s band, this was about 1961, we used to rehearse at Birdland. And Maynard called a 4:00 rehearsal. Well Basie had called a 1:00 rehearsal. So I got there a little early and Basie’s band was still rehearsing. Well Frank Wess was playing second alto then. I don’t know if you remember that configuration. But I think it was Billy Mitchell and Frank Foster were playing the other two tenors. But Frank Wess didn’t show up so Marshall said, “you want to come over here and play a couple of tunes with us to finish out the rehearsal?” I said, “sure.” So I went up and played with them and we played through this thing, it was sort of mediocre. And Ernie Wilkins had brought this chart in. Well now Ernie Wilkins is the one that wrote “Geller’s Cellar” which later became “Morgan’s Organ” that I recorded with Maynard’s band. But it was originally written for Herb Geller. But anyway we got through playing this and Marshall looked at Ernie, standing right in front of the band and he said, “Ernie, who wrote this piece of shit?” And Ernie says, “what do you mean, Marsh,” he said, “I wrote it. What’s wrong with it?” Marshall said, “Ernie, that’s the worst piece of crap I ever heard, man.” He said, “who wrote this, Ernie?” And Ernie said, “I wrote it.” Marshall says, “I’ll be God damned if you wrote it.” That’s the only time I ever — now I never knew who did it, but I’ve got a hunch Marshall was right. He didn’t have time and he farmed it out to somebody. Maybe he had a kid, one of his students or something write it and played him a couple of bucks and took it in. But Marshall nailed him right away. And he would do that. He became a little more mellow in his older years. But he was a funny guy. And he and Rabbit [Johnny Hodges] they used to play the same way. They’d play with their eyes open, and they’d play something that was hot you know, something that they thought would get all the ladies and so forth, and then they’d go — and they’d kind of look all around like this. It’s really wild to watch. It’s that school.
Yeah. I can see Johnny Hodges doing that. I didn’t know Marshall did that.
Marshall did it too. It was very funny. I used to watch them and I wouldn’t crack up but I would inside.
Hey — I’ll have to try that someday. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
